exercises.title: Equal is not older
exercises.brief:
Write stale_by_time, deciding whether an output must be rebuilt, given the output's timestamp and the timestamps of its inputs.

Rebuild when any input is at least as new as the output. Equal counts, because two files written in the same tick are indistinguishable and the safe reading of a tie is that the input may have come second.

An output with no inputs is never stale. An output that does not exist yet has a timestamp of 0 and must be built.
exercises.concept: The two errors are not symmetric, so a tie is resolved towards over-building, which costs time, rather than towards under-building, which costs correctness.
hints: The comparison that looks right is strictly newer, and it is the one that loses eight builds out of ten.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. An input whose timestamp equals the output's has to count as stale. Requiring it to be strictly newer is exactly the granularity failure: two files written in the same second compare equal and the build declines.

exercises.after: Measured on ten rapid edit and rebuild cycles with a one second clock, eight produced a binary that did not match the source, in silence.

exercises.title: Time that moves backwards
exercises.brief:
Write time_model_fails, deciding whether a timestamp based build system will under-build, given the previous and current content hashes of an input and its previous and current timestamps.

The system rebuilds when the timestamp moved forwards. It under-builds when the content changed and the timestamp did not move forwards, which is what extracting an archive or restoring a backup does.

Return 1 for an under-build and 0 otherwise.
exercises.concept: This is not a bug in one tool. Any system whose cache key is a timestamp has it, because the key is not a function of the content.
hints: Two questions: did the content change, and would the timestamp have made the system notice.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Content that changed while the timestamp went backwards, or stayed the same, is the silent case. Content that did not change is never an under-build, however the timestamp moved.

exercises.after: Give a header new content and a timestamp from 2020 and every timestamp based system on earth says there is nothing to do.

exercises.title: A key, not a comparison
exercises.brief:
Write cache_key_hit, deciding whether a content addressed build system can skip a node, given the hash of its inputs, the hash of its command, the hash of the environment it depends on, and the same three values recorded when the output was made.

All three have to match. Any difference is a different key, and a different key is a miss.
exercises.concept: The command line is not a file, so a timestamp cannot see it change. A key made from the command can.
hints: Three comparisons, all of which have to hold.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Changing the optimisation level changes the command hash and nothing else, and a system that only compares the inputs happily reuses an object built with different flags.

exercises.after: A plain make sees no file newer than any other when the flags change, so it does nothing, and the tree ends up half built one way and half the other.

exercises.title: Stopping when nothing changed
exercises.brief:
Write downstream_runs, returning how many downstream nodes must run in a chain of n nodes, given whether each node's output came out byte identical to what was there before.

A node runs when the node before it produced something different. If a node's output is unchanged, nothing after it needs to run, and the propagation stops there. The first node always runs, because its input is what you edited.

same[i] is non-zero when node i produced an identical output. Count the nodes that run, including the first.
exercises.concept: Early cutoff is what a timestamp cannot express, because a timestamp records that work happened rather than whether the result differs.
hints: Walk forwards and stop at the first node whose output was unchanged.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Editing a comment recompiles the object and produces the same bytes, so the link does not need to happen. Counting the whole chain is what a timestamp system does.

exercises.after: On a large tree this is the difference between a rebuild you wait for and one you do not notice.

exercises.title: The header nobody declared
exercises.brief:
Write edge_missing, deciding whether a build will under-build after a header edit, given whether the rule declares the header and whether the compiler generated a dependency file that does.

The graph has the edge if either the rule names it or a generated dependency file names it. Without the edge, the object does not rebuild and the binary stops matching the source.
exercises.concept: The compiler is the only party that knows which headers were actually read, which is why the dependency list is a side effect of compiling rather than something a person maintains.
hints: Either source of the edge is enough. Only having neither is a problem.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. A generated dependency file supplies the edge just as well as a hand written rule, which is the entire point of generating it.

exercises.after: A project without generated dependencies has this bug today, and it shows up as a header edit that changes nothing until somebody builds from clean.

exercises.title: What infinitely many cores cannot buy
exercises.brief:
Write critical_path, returning the length of the longest chain of work in a build graph, given each node's cost and the index of the node it depends on.

Node i depends on dep[i], or on nothing when dep[i] is -1. A node cannot start until what it depends on has finished. Every node's dependency has a lower index than the node itself.
exercises.concept: The total work is what one core takes. The critical path is what infinitely many take, and the gap is all that parallelism can buy.
hints: The finish time of a node is its own cost plus the finish time of what it waits for. The answer is the largest finish time.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Summing every cost gives what a single core takes, which is the other number. Two independent chains do not add together on a wide machine.

exercises.after: This is why a header included everywhere makes a build slow on any machine: everything waits for the same node, and no number of cores shortens a chain.

exercises.title: Which nodes may run now
exercises.brief:
Write ready_nodes, returning how many nodes of a build graph can start immediately, given for each node how many of its dependencies have not finished yet, and whether it has already been built.

A node is ready when it has not been built and nothing it depends on is outstanding. This is the width of the graph at this moment, and it is what limits how many cores are worth having right now.
exercises.concept: A build system walks a graph. Everything else it does is a consequence of which nodes are ready and which are not.
hints: A node that is already built is not ready. It is finished.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Counting nodes with no outstanding dependencies includes the ones already built, which reports work that does not exist and, in a real scheduler, runs it a second time.

exercises.after: The width changes as the build proceeds, which is why a build that starts wide can end on one core waiting for a single link.

exercises.title: Naming the failure
exercises.brief:
Write classify, returning which kind of build failure occurred, given whether the node was rebuilt and whether its inputs had actually changed.

Return 1 for an under-build, which is a rebuild that should have happened and did not; 2 for an over-build, which is work that was not needed; and 0 when the decision was right.
exercises.concept: The words are worth having, because one of these is a slow build and the other is a wrong program that no tool reports.
hints: Two booleans, four cases, and two of them are correct.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Rebuilding something that did not need it is an over-build and costs only time. Not rebuilding something that did need it is the silent one.

exercises.after: A clean build is not a fix for either. If building from scratch differs from building incrementally, an edge is missing, and that is the thing to find.
